summary: Defines a way to send Online Certificate Status Protocol responses in-band within Kerberos. These responses confirm that the certificates used in PKINIT are still valid. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: Before accepting an ID card, you want to know it was not cancelled. This lets the answer to that check travel along with the login messages.

questions: how does pkinit check certificate revocation
what pre-authentication type is 18 in kerberos
subtitle: Lets Kerberos clients and servers carry fresh certificate status answers inside PKINIT login messages.

tldr.problem: Constrained clients may want to check whether a KDC certificate has been revoked without downloading large Certificate Revocation Lists.
tldr.mechanism: A new pre-authentication type, PA-PK-OCSP-RESPONSE (18), carries one or more OCSP responses alongside the PKINIT exchange, in both directions.
tldr.outcome: Clients and the KDC can reuse cached OCSP responses and check certificates without CRLs. The extension is optional and does not itself authenticate anyone.

today: RFC 4557 is a Proposed Standard from June 2006. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP, RFC 2560) lets applications get timely information on whether a certificate has been revoked. OCSP responses are well bounded and small, so constrained clients may prefer them over downloading large Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs) when checking the certificates of a Kerberos Key Distribution Center (KDC). That saves bandwidth on constrained networks.

RFC 4557 defines a pre-authentication type, as in RFC 4120, in which the client and the KDC MAY piggyback OCSP responses for certificates used in the authentication exchanges of PKINIT (RFC 4556). The extension is OPTIONAL, and it lets both sides reuse cached OCSP responses.
sections.eli5: Instead of fetching a huge list of cancelled ID cards, you get a short note that says whether this one card is still good.

sections.title: The PA-PK-OCSP-RESPONSE Message
sections.content:
The new pre-authentication type is PA-PK-OCSP-RESPONSE, with identifier 18. Its padata-value holds the DER encoding of a PKOcspData, which is a sequence of OcspResponse. Each OcspResponse is an octet string holding one complete OCSP response as defined in RFC 2560.

If more than one response is included, the first MUST be the response for the signer's certificate. The signer is the client in the AS-REQ and the KDC in the AS-REP.
sections.eli5: The message is a small envelope holding one or more certificate-check answers. The first answer must be about the sender's own card.

sections.title: How Clients and KDCs Use It
sections.content:
The client MAY send OCSP responses for the certificates used in PA-PK-AS-REQ. A KDC that receives a PA-PK-OCSP-RESPONSE SHOULD send back one with OCSP responses for the certificates used in its PA-PK-AS-REP. A client can ask for one by sending a PKOcspData containing an empty sequence. The KDC MAY also send one even if the client sent none.

The OCSP response is signed by the OCSP server, which the receiver trusts. Depending on local policy, further checking of the OCSP servers may be needed.

Both sides SHOULD ignore invalid OCSP responses received this way. They MAY fall back to CRL processing if the responses alone do not settle certificate validity, and they MAY ignore a valid response and do their own revocation checking.
sections.eli5: You can hand over a revocation note, or hand over an empty envelope to ask the other side for theirs. If a note looks bad, you may throw it away and check another way.

sections.title: Missing or Empty Responses
sections.content:
The empty or missing OCSP response has no integrity protection. The RFC therefore says that a client SHOULD treat a missing expected OCSP response for the KDC's certificates as an error, unless it is configured otherwise.

More generally, if a PKINIT client or KDC cannot validate certificates without a valid PA-PK-OCSP-RESPONSE, it SHOULD fail the AS exchange, possibly according to local configuration.
sections.eli5: If you expected a note saying the card is good and no note comes, you should be suspicious and may refuse to go on.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The pre-authentication data defined here does not authenticate any principal. It is meant to be used together with PKINIT. The only binding between it and the PKINIT data is that an OCSP response corresponds to a certificate used in a PKINIT element.

Because of this, removing or replacing PA-PK-OCSP-RESPONSE elements is at worst a downgrade attack, where a client or KDC proceeds without CRLs or OCSP, or a denial-of-service attack, where a party that cannot validate the other's certificate without an OCSP response rejects the exchange or must download very large CRLs. Kerberos V does not protect against denial of service, so the RFC calls that aspect acceptable.
sections.eli5: Someone could remove the note so you skip the check, or so you have to do extra work. The RFC accepts that risk and says to stop the login if you cannot check the card.

messages.label: PA-PK-AS-REQ + PA-PK-OCSP-RESPONSE
messages.note: Optional; an empty sequence asks the KDC for its responses.

messages.label: PA-PK-AS-REP + PA-PK-OCSP-RESPONSE
messages.note: Covers the certificates used in the PA-PK-AS-REP.
